hook: Vladimir Vapnik developed much of the mathematical foundation that modern machine learning still relies on. Born in Tashkent in the Soviet Union, he earned his doctorate in statistics from the Institute of Control Sciences in Moscow in 1964, where he later headed the computer science research department. Working with Alexey Chervonenkis, he developed what became known as Vapnik-Chervonenkis theory, a mathematical framework for understanding when and why a learning algorithm can generalize from training data to new examples. After moving to the United States, he joined AT&T Bell Labs, where he and colleagues including Corinna Cortes, Bernard Boser, and Isabelle Guyon turned his theoretical work into the support vector machine, a classification method described in a landmark 1995 paper with Cortes and in a US patent he shares with Boser and Guyon. He went on to hold research and teaching positions at NEC Laboratories, Royal Holloway University of London, Columbia University, and Facebook AI Research, continuing to develop and extend statistical learning theory.

quick_facts: Co-developed Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) theory with Alexey Chervonenkis, a foundational framework in statistical learning theory
Co-invented the support vector machine, described with Corinna Cortes in a 1995 paper in the journal Machine Learning
Named inventor on a 1997 US patent for a pattern recognition system using support vectors, along with Bernard Boser and Isabelle Guyon
Elected to the US National Academy of Engineering in 1996
Has held research and academic positions at AT&T Bell Labs, NEC Laboratories, Royal Holloway University of London, Columbia University, and Facebook AI Research
Received the Benjamin Franklin Medal in Computer and Cognitive Science in 2012 for his contributions to machine learning

achievements.title: Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) theory
achievements.impact: Provided the mathematical basis for understanding when a learning algorithm can generalize from a finite set of examples to new data, a cornerstone of statistical learning theory.

achievements.title: Support vector machine
achievements.impact: Created, with collaborators at AT&T Bell Labs, a classification algorithm that became one of the most widely used machine learning methods before the rise of deep learning.

achievements.title: Support-Vector Networks paper (1995)
achievements.impact: Co-authored with Corinna Cortes the paper introducing the soft margin support vector machine, extending the method to handle data that cannot be perfectly separated.

achievements.title: Statistical learning theory books
achievements.impact: Wrote The Nature of Statistical Learning Theory and Statistical Learning Theory, texts that formalized the theory behind generalization for a generation of researchers.
